TRANSCRIPT OF PROCEEDINGS
THE HON CATHERINE HOLMES AC SC, Commissioner
THE ROYAL COMMISSION INTO THE ROBODEBT SCHEME
TUESDAY, 21 FEBRUARY 2023 AT 10:00 AM (AEST)
DAY 33
MR JUSTIN GREGGERY KC, Senior Counsel Assisting
MS SALWA MARSH, Counsel Assisting
MS DOMINIQUE HOGAN-DORAN SC, for the Commonwealth
MR TRENT GLOVER, for the Commonwealth
MR ALEXANDRE VIAL, for the Commonwealth
MR FLYNN, for Ms Kathryn Campbell

COMMISSIONER: I will just take the appearances to begin with, Mr Greggery?
MR GREGGERY: Yes. Thank you, Commissioner. This morning I appear with Ms Marsh of
Counsel.
COMMISSIONER: Thank you. Ms Hogan-Doran?
MS HOGAN-DORAN: Thank you, Commissioner. This morning I appear with Mr Glover. Later
this afternoon when Mr Roser is called, Mr Glover and Mr Vial will take him.
COMMISSIONER: Thank you. And it's Mr Flynn, is it? Thanks, Mr Flynn. Yes.
MR FLYNN: Commissioner, we put in an application for leave to cross-examine. That may
have been overtaken by events in the Supplementary Statement. We just reserve the
position.
COMMISSIONER: Sure. I saw your application, and it was approved. So if you need to, play it
by ear.
MR FLYNN: May it please the Commission.
COMMISSIONER: Yes, Mr Greggery.
MR GREGGERY: Yes. Thank you, Commissioner. The first witness is Paul Menzies-McVey, who
is present.
COMMISSIONER: Right. Mr Menzies-McVey, would you prefer to take an oath or an
affirmation?
MR MENZIES-McVEY: Affirmation.
COMMISSIONER: All right. Would you stand?
<PAUL ALEXANDER RICHARD MENZIES-MCVEY, AFFIRMED
<EXAMINATION BY MR GREGGERY:
MR GREGGERY: Can you tell the Commission your full name, please.
MR MENZIES-McVEY: Paul Alexander Richard Menzies-McVey.
MR GREGGERY: Mr Menzies-McVey, you were served with NTG-0162, a Notice to Give a
Statement and Produce Documents, dated 13 January 2023. And you produced a Statement
in response dated 24 January 2023 and a Supplementary Statement dated 18 February 2023.
Is that correct?

MR MENZIES-McVEY: That's correct.
MR GREGGERY: There is a bundle of material before you which will include those
Statements, that Notice and other documents to which I may take you. Commissioner, I take
it you have a draft witness - sorry, exhibit list for the day?
COMMISSIONER: Yes, I do.
MR GREGGERY: It's convenient at this point, even though Ms Marsh will take the evidence of
Ms Blake and Mr Scott will later take the evidence of Mr Roser, that I tender the exhibits on
the draft list in the entirety at this point. It commences number 5269 and concludes number
5351.
COMMISSIONER: Yes. Those exhibits are admitted with the descriptions they bear in the list.
Thank you.
<EXHIBITS 2569 TO 5351 TENDERED AS PER THE EXHIBIT LIST
MR GREGGERY: Mr Menzies-McVey, the period with which your Statement - first Statement
is initially concerned is early January 2017; that's correct?
MR MENZIES-McVEY: That's correct.
MR GREGGERY: And at that point in time, you were acting in a position of some seniority
within the Department of Human Services in the legal area?
MR MENZIES-McVEY: That's correct. I was a Senior Executive Band 1 on an ongoing basis, but
for a period of one week just after the Christmas vacation I was Acting Chief Counsel.
MR GREGGERY: And who were you replacing?
MR MENZIES-McVEY: Annette Musolino.
MR GREGGERY: Other people were acting in the Department at that point in time, I think at
Deputy Secretary and Secretary level?
MR MENZIES-McVEY: That's correct. I think there is often a period of leave around Christmas
and so there is quite a lot of acting in that period.
MR GREGGERY: Was it Mr Barry Jackson who was acting Secretary?
MR MENZIES-McVEY: I believe so, yes.
MR GREGGERY: All right. And so far as you were concerned, was it Ms Sue Kruse who was
Acting Deputy Secretary?

MR GREGGERY: And to your knowledge, was she acting in the place of Mr Jonathan Hutson?
MR MENZIES-McVEY: I believe so.
MR GREGGERY: Okay. Now, as you indicate in your first Statement, you - from April 2016
until March 2017, you were the Branch Manager of the Business Transformation Legal
Branch, which is one of six legal branches?
MR MENZIES-McVEY: At the time, yes, that's correct.
MR GREGGERY: And how many lawyers were in the Business Transformation Legal Branch?
MR MENZIES-McVEY: It was a relatively small Branch. I think there would have been
potentially 12, 13 lawyers.
MR GREGGERY: And when you say that's relatively small, is that compared to the five other
legal branches?
MR MENZIES-McVEY: Some of the other branches were very large, yes. And so I think there
was approximately 200 people all told in the Legal Services Division. So my Branch was a
relatively small part of that overall workforce.
MR GREGGERY: Right. Now, you say that your role in that position was to provide strategic
legal advice on major business - there is a typographical error, but transportation projects or
transformation projects.
MR MENZIES-McVEY: Transformation projects that should be, yes. So there was a very large
program colloquially known as WPIT, the Welfare Payments Transformation Program, in
which the Department was seeking to acquire technology that would enable it to provide
services in a - for - principally for the Centrelink program, but also for other government
programs, in a more efficient way. There was also sort of a major telecommunications
contract that related to the very sophisticated telephone system that the Department used
to deal with incoming telephone inquiries, and my Branch provided assistance with the
management of that contract.
MR GREGGERY: The WPIT program was an expensive program in the sense that it updated
much of the information technology of the Centrelink office.
MR MENZIES-McVEY: That's correct.
MR GREGGERY: Which, at that stage, was outdated or becoming outdated?
MR MENZIES-McVEY: It was becoming much more difficult to keep up to date, and I think
one of the other issues was that it wasn't particularly flexible. And so as the government
wished to, you know, deliver programs in a different way, they were often told that the

program was intended to provide a degree of agility, I think, to the way that the Department
was able to deliver services and particularly make payments.
MR GREGGERY: In a period of at least a number of years, there were various upgrades
proposed under the WPIT program?
MR MENZIES-McVEY: Yes. When I was in - as you, I think, mentioned, I was - I left the
Department in March 2017. And so at that stage, we were - it was to be in the early stages of
the WPIT program. And so there were - there was procurement being done, but there
wasn't - you know, at that stage, I don't think there was technology in place to - you know, to
be the early stages of the program. So it's a lot of planning and a lot of procurement.
MR GREGGERY: In respect of the planning and the procurement side of things for WPIT, were
you kept updated about costing of the procurement and costing of the projected
implementation?
MR MENZIES-McVEY: I think - I don't think I was a recipient of a specific report on that, but I
sort of knew in broad terms, you know, how much money was going to be involved in the
various components because that was relevant to the procurement documents that we were
assisting other consultants to put together.
MR GREGGERY: Like with any substantial expenditure, did you understand that that
expenditure in terms of the Department's obligations, at least in Budget rounds, required
funding or savings?
MR MENZIES-McVEY: I wasn't closely involved - or, in fact, that's probably overstating it. I
wasn't involved in the - putting together the Budget bids for the WPIT program, but I was
aware that the government had decided to provide Budget funding for that program. So it
wasn't being absorbed by the Department, it was - there was the actual specific allocated
Budget funding for the program.
MR GREGGERY: Did you ever become aware in your role in respect of WPIT of any
relationship between the Online Compliance Intervention Scheme or the Debt Recovery
Scheme that commenced as a Budget Measure in 2015 and funding for the WPIT program?
MR MENZIES-McVEY: No, I wasn't.
MR GREGGERY: During the week that you acted in Ms Musolino's position in early January
2017, I take it you recall the significant publicity surrounding the Debt Recovery Scheme
which was then underway?
MR MENZIES-McVEY: Until I reviewed the emails, I must say I didn't recall the publicity. But it
did seem that one of the - I did - when I was looking at emails, there seemed to be quite a
few media stories about - reported on that - on the Robodebt program in that period. So - - -
MR GREGGERY: I take it from your answer you still don't recall that, but you see it recorded

MR MENZIES-McVEY: Yes. I mean, I have a general understanding that the media was
interested at Robodebt at various points. I must say I didn't know exactly when that period
was because I wasn't normally involved with the Robodebt program, so it wasn't sort of part
of my business as usual. But, I mean, it's - the email trails show that there was a lot of media
around that time, so - and I'm perfectly happy to accept that, yes.
MR GREGGERY: What about your recollection of the Ombudsman's involvement? Do you
have any independent recollection of discussing matters or meeting with the Ombudsman or
representatives of that office?
MR MENZIES-McVEY: I am aware from the review of the emails that I did meet with - or
there was a meeting with the Ombudsman. I think I attended it. I don't have a recollection of
what was said at that meeting, although I do have an email that seems to have - I did see an
email that seemed to result in part at least from that meeting. So, yes, I assume that I
attended, but I don't recall what I - what the meeting covered.
MR GREGGERY: What about any independent recollection of the fact that Minister Porter
was acting in the position of Minister Tudge during the period that you were acting in
Ms Musolino's position?
MR MENZIES-McVEY: I - if you say that's the case, I'm happy to accept it. But I have no
knowledge of that and - I'm sorry, I didn't - I don't recall.
MR GREGGERY: What about any independent recollection of a Senate inquiry into the
Scheme in early 2017 when you returned to your substantive position?
MR MENZIES-McVEY: I - I don't. I was - when I returned to my substantive position, I
remained at the Department until March in which - when I went on to another role. So I may
not have had particular focus on - on the Robodebt program. At the time in the Business
Transformation Legal Branch, there was a lot of activity. And so I think my focus was very
much on the role of my Branch.
MR GREGGERY: And does that include the publicity surrounding the Ombudsman's
investigation after you stopped acting in Ms Musolino's position? That is, you don't have any
independent recollection of it?
MR MENZIES-McVEY: No, I do not.
MR GREGGERY: Your Statement indicates that you left the Department in March 2017 and
then returned and took up a role in July 2018 with the Department of Social Services. Is that
the sequence?
MR MENZIES-McVEY: Yes. I went - I left the Department of Human Services in March 2017
and went to work at an IT company.

MR MENZIES-McVEY: No - so when you say "return", I mean, I hadn't previously been at DSS.
MR GREGGERY: Hadn't been at DSS, no.
MR MENZIES-McVEY: But the - when I joined DSS, I - initially I worked as a Senior Executive
Branch Manager but in a policy role that had nothing to do with the Legal Services team at
DSS.
MR GREGGERY: And then you came to be involved into the DSS Legal Services Branch directly
in about May 2019.
MR MENZIES-McVEY: That's correct.
MR GREGGERY: So about two years and two or three months after you left DSS, you were
back into the legal stream.
MR MENZIES-McVEY: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: And when you returned to the legal stream in May 2019 in DSS, Kathryn
Campbell was the Secretary of DSS?
MR MENZIES-McVEY: That's correct.
MR GREGGERY: Nathan Williamson was a Deputy Secretary at DSS?
MR MENZIES-McVEY: Correct.
MR GREGGERY: Both of those persons were in Secretary and Deputy Secretary roles at DHS
when you were there in January 2017?
MR MENZIES-McVEY: Certainly Kathryn Campbell was the Secretary. Nathan Williamson was
certainly there. I'm just not sure whether he was a Deputy Secretary when I was there in
2017, but I'm happy to accept that he was if that's the case.
MR GREGGERY: All right.
MR MENZIES-McVEY: He was - - -
MR GREGGERY: And soon after you took up that role as a Deputy Chief Counsel in DSS Legal
Services Branch in May 2019, you became aware that DSS had obtained some advice from
Clayton Utz in respect of the Debt Recovery Scheme implemented by DHS?
MR MENZIES-McVEY: That's correct. It wasn't immediately after I became the Deputy Chief
Counsel, but it was a relatively short period after.

MR MENZIES-McVEY: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: Yes. Now, when you took up that role in May 2019, were you aware or did
you very soon become aware of litigation in the Federal Court in respect of Ms Masterton?
MR MENZIES-McVEY: Yes, I was. I think I became aware of - it was in the context of me
understanding or getting up to speed, as it were, on the current - current Federal Court
matter in Masterton.
MR GREGGERY: Yes.
MR MENZIES-McVEY: But I was trying to understand the issues raised by that pace and
significance of it, and I think it - at that point, I became aware of the draft Clayton Utz advice.
MR GREGGERY: And how did you become aware of that?
MR MENZIES-McVEY: It was conveyed to me by - I mean, the Branch had a number of
different teams attributed to a number of different types of work. So one of those teams
was - did social security law advice, and I think that team provided me with a number of
briefing documents about how it all worked and what we did in relation to matters with
Services Australia. And this was a part of that bundle of things I received as sort of like a - it
was a sort of induction, but it was just sort of learning how the - how that part of the Branch
worked.
MR GREGGERY: And how big was the social security law part of that Branch?
MR MENZIES-McVEY: It had between - it varied, but between, say, five or six people in
most - and so the total Branch was of the order of 35 to 40, depending on whether you count
the lawyers - any lawyers or - and support staff as well. But the social security team was a
sort of a small part of that overall Branch structure. And so my time was sort of shared
between the various teams of the Branch.
MR GREGGERY: The induction or briefing that you received soon after you commenced in
that position, was that provided in an email to you with various attachments?
MR MENZIES-McVEY: No. I think when I first went to the Branch, I tried to have a lot of sort
of face-to-face chats with people in the Branch. As a new Branch Manager, it's sort of a - my
feeling was that was the best way to sort of introduce myself to the team and so people
could understand, and I could ask questions. And so the - while it's entirely possible that
some documents, including the draft Clayton Utz advice, were emailed to me or handed to
me in hard copy, I think most of my briefing was sort of in the nature of an oral briefing.
MR GREGGERY: Were you surprised when you received a copy of the Clayton Utz advice?
MR MENZIES-McVEY: I was.

MR GREGGERY: And does that emotional response indicate that you can recall how you
received it?
MR MENZIES-McVEY: No, I remember given access to it. As I say, I don't know whether that
was a hard copy or an email, but I did then read it. And it was - it was surprising to me
that - that that - you know, the advice was a draft advice and obtained from Clayton Utz in
that way. So - - -
MR GREGGERY: What do you mean by that?
MR MENZIES-McVEY: Well, the - if an advice was - there are a couple of things about the
advice that I thought were sort of worthy of note in my mind. The first is - and this may
potentially have been because I have, you know, experience at DHS and sort of understood
that, you know, often the way the programs are delivered is very complicated, and DSS
sometimes doesn't know all the intricacies of every paragraph, of every letter that might be
sent to customers and what have you. So it seemed surprising that the Clayton Utz advice
had been obtained without consultation with Services Australia because they would be able
to much better inform Clayton Utz about the exact chain of events and what letters would
have been sent to the person.
The second thing about the Clayton Utz advice is, from recollection, it was just an advice
about an AAT1 - a particular AAT1 matter that didn't seem to - and Clayton Utz didn't seem
to have been instructed about the correspondence that may have been sent to this person,
and they weren't asked to advise about whether there was any legal implications from the
fact that people may - the customer may have received correspondence prior to the debt
being raised. The other thing that I thought was interesting was that the advice was sought
from Clayton Utz and - you know, Clayton Utz is a very highly respected law firm in
administrative law.
But if an advice that was going towards the issue of whether a program was sort of being
conducted properly that was a sort of a Cabinet - well, a major government program, I would
have expected the advice to have been sought from AGS rather than from Clayton Utz, if only
because if the matter needed to be escalated to a Minister or Cabinet down the track, then
AGS advice would have been required. And so getting advice from Clayton Utz would have
possibly just been only a first step of what would need to have been a two-step process. So I
would have thought that if DSS was concerned about the program at some point, it's
perfectly appropriate to get advice but probably in consultation with Services Australia
providing a full briefing to the legal service provider about how the program worked. And,
you know, I expect advice from AGS that the advice could be seen as authoritative on that
point.
MR GREGGERY: These were all views you formed upon reading the advice within a few
weeks of coming into the role?
MR MENZIES-McVEY: Yes.

MR GREGGERY: What questions did you ask then about all of those issues of the social
security law team?
MR MENZIES-McVEY: I - my - I kept that - you know, this advice that people within the
Department knew of the existence of the draft advice, and I understood that from the
answer from social security team to be that people were aware of the draft advice. Had - at
that stage, a decision had been made to brief the Solicitor-General to provide advice on the
Income Compliance Program. And if - and so I thought that the - in a sense, events had sort
of overtaken the Clayton Utz advice. Because if the Solicitor-General was going to provide
advice, it would be regarded as completely authoritative within the Commonwealth about
the lawfulness or lack thereof of the program. And so the - in a sense, the Clayton Utz advice
was something that was of no - no longer of future sort of significance in terms of guiding the
Department or - about this matter because within - I thought within a period of a couple of
months - as it turned out, it was a little bit longer than that, but I thought within a period of a
month or two we would have a definitive advice from the Solicitor-General about the
program.
MR GREGGERY: But at that point in time, in May or June, the Solicitor-General had not yet
been briefed.
MR MENZIES-McVEY: No, that - the Solicitor-General hadn't been briefed, but a decision had
been made that he would be briefed. And so the actual process of briefing the
Solicitor-General seemed to have been delayed a little by the election around May that year.
And so there was a - I think Services Australia were of the view that it was important that the
Minister, whoever that might be post-election, was aware that advice was going to be
obtained from the Solicitor-General on the program. And so there was a pause during the
election campaign until a Minister was sworn in before proceeding to get the advice. But
my - as soon as - I think my recollection is that very shortly after the Minister was sworn in
post-election, the Minister confirmed the advice should be obtained and work was
underway, you know, from that point to prepare necessary questions, observations,
supporting documents.
MR GREGGERY: You are giving evidence there about your belief of the state of mind or
collective state of mind of Services Australia. What was the view of DSS about the question?
MR MENZIES-McVEY: Are you asking me whether things should have paused during the
election campaign or - - -
MR GREGGERY: Yes.
MR MENZIES-McVEY: I - I don't know what - I can't speak for DSS. I can speak for myself. And
so my - I remember thinking that I wasn't sure this is something that the - yes, that the
caretaker conventions would necessarily prevent happening in the sense that bureaucrats
were just planning legal advice on an existing program, as opposed to some future program.
But at the same time, it - you know, there seemed to be - I was relatively confident that the
advice would be obtained post-election. So, yes, there might have been a six-week delay or

something, which is, in my view, not ideal, but it didn't seem to me to be a sort of a
fundamental problem that needed that - you know, needed some intervention on my part.
COMMISSIONER: Sorry. Can I just ask: that Clayton Utz advice had been sitting around in DSS
since August the previous year. You are looking at it in about June 2019?
MR MENZIES-McVEY: Yes, it would have been sort of late - Commissioner, I think it would
have been sort of late May, early June. Yes.
COMMISSIONER: Right. Did you ask what on earth had been happening with it?
MR MENZIES-McVEY: I didn't ask as to what decisions were made not to take it out of - you
know, to progress it from its draft state. My view would have been but for the fact that the
Solicitor-General's advice was going to be obtained, which sort of made this sort of
consideration less relevant, I think I would have said to DSS, "Well, it's probably not good to
have a draft advice sitting there just not complete because it clearly doesn't completely
advise on the issue," because it didn't deal with what legal significance, if any, the - sort of
the correspondence process with the - with the customer had.
And so the option would have been to either go back to Clayton Utz and provide them with a
better briefing and ask some further questions or, alternatively, which would have been my
preference, to go to AGS and ask them a complete set of questions about the program. But
as I mentioned to - in evidence to Mr Greggery - in answer to Mr Greggery's questions, I
thought that this issue in a sense had been overtaken by the fact that when - when the
Commonwealth was already on underway in getting sort of, like, the definitive legal advice,
that would sort of, you know, be the only legal advice that the Commonwealth would rely
upon. So in the sense I didn't need to go back and explore that history because sort of a
better result was already underway.
COMMISSIONER: But you have this advice which says that the Act does not accommodate
averaging. That's the effect of it, that averaging is not a thing you can do under the Social
Security Act. Just wait. Somebody in your Department has received that advice in August the
previous year and absolutely nothing has happened. Is that not a concern? Do you not worry
about the practices of the Department and make some inquiries to see how did that
happen?
MR MENZIES-McVEY: I - I didn't undertake an investigation of the circumstances of that,
Commissioner.
COMMISSIONER: Did you just ask anybody what happened?
MR MENZIES-McVEY: I - I don't recall doing that. The - I think that - I personally don't like
having draft advices because their status is sort of unclear.
COMMISSIONER: Never mind the status, what about the content? This is a bit of a concern
because it is saying that a program which the government has been operating for a couple of

MR MENZIES-McVEY: Commissioner, I think what I would say is that I don't think the
advice - I mean, it certainly is a very important point that the way that social security benefits
are calculated in social security law requires evidence of actual earnings, not averaged
earnings. That's a completely, you know, important point. The Clayton Utz advice, from my
recollection, did not engage at all with the - whether the engagement with the customer
prior to a debt being raised properly allowed decision-makers to draw inferences from the
customer's lack of engagement.
And so I wouldn't characterise that advice as saying that the program was unlawful. I think
it's making a very important point about how social security law is drafted, but it - there's a
distinction between that and saying that the Income Compliance Program itself was sort
of - led to unlawful consequences because of this extra step that - the Solicitor-General
ultimately advised that the extra step didn't have significance, but I think that was a
fair - sort of a very real legal issue.
And so I certainly can say that but for the fact that the Solicitor-General was going to be
instructed to provide advice, I would have felt uncomfortable about that advice staying as a
draft advice and not being completed. I would have either provided - asked Clayton Utz to do
further advice in a more complete way or in consultation with Services Australia, or had
asked preferably AGS to do a more complete advice on it. But I didn't have to do that
because - - -
COMMISSIONER: Because you were going to get the Solicitor-General's opinion.
MR MENZIES-McVEY: Solicitor-General's advice.
COMMISSIONER: You've told us that. What I'm more interested in is why were you
comfortable with people in your Department apparently being prepared to let this thing just
sit there for almost a year without action, without asking a few questions about how does
that happen, who takes responsibility for this?
MR MENZIES-McVEY: Commissioner, I think that I was sort of looking towards managing the
current and future issues - legal issues. I wasn't - didn't have the mindset of sort of - sort of, I
guess, examining prior activities of the Legal Services Branch. And so the - I - there was a lot
to do going forward. And so I guess I was looking in a forward direction rather than a rear
direction, and it wasn't the normal practice of - I mean, I would have been quite concerned
had we sort of - under my term as Branch Manager if that sort of - negative draft advices
were obtained and just let to sit on the file. But I - it's my - I'm not aware of any instances
when I was a Branch Manager where that happened. So it's not as though I was thinking this
is a - you know, there is some bad practices in the Branch I need to get rid of. I think all the
lawyers in the Branch are very capable and conscientious. And so I didn't feel like there
was - - -
COMMISSIONER: You didn't see an issue there.

COMMISSIONER: All right. Thank you.
MR GREGGERY: Well, by this time, the Department also - as I think you said, was aware of
the Masterton proceedings and you were - - -
MR MENZIES-McVEY: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: - - - looking into that. Undoubtedly, you became aware of an advice from
Mr Ensbey dated 27 March 2019 in respect of the Masterton proceedings?
MR MENZIES-McVEY: Belatedly.
MR GREGGERY: What do you mean "belatedly"?
MR MENZIES-McVEY: I think I received a copy of that advice sort of late in June, so it was
somewhat after it was produced.
MR GREGGERY: And how were you shown a copy of that?
MR MENZIES-McVEY: I believe I obtained it from a Branch Manager in Services Australia, the
Litigation Branch Manager, whose name is currently escaping me. But - - -
MR GREGGERY: Mr Ffrench?
MR MENZIES-McVEY: No, it wasn't Mr Ffrench. Maybe - it was a Branch Manager of the - of
the Litigation Branch at Services Australia. And, ideally, that advice would have been shared
with us earlier because we were interested in the Masterton proceedings, and it would have
been sort of useful to have seen that advice at an earlier point.
MR GREGGERY: When you say you received it in June, are you giving that evidence from
recollection, or have you looked at a document?
MR MENZIES-McVEY: There is a - I think I have seen an email. I have - sorry, I have seen an
email where that was sent to me in June.
MR GREGGERY: Is that an email that you included in a reference in your Statement?
MR MENZIES-McVEY: I don't believe so.
MR GREGGERY: All right. Is it the case that you reviewed your emails for the period from
when you commenced the Deputy Chief Counsel role in May 2019 through to the end of the
year - - -
MR MENZIES-McVEY: Yes.

MR MENZIES-McVEY: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: All right. What emails did you identify about how the Clayton Utz advice was
provided to you?
MR MENZIES-McVEY: The - I did search to see whether I could see an email where it was sent
to me in that period from late May, early June. I couldn't see an email from that. So, as I have
stated previously, it may have been given to me as a hard copy following a conversation.
So - I certainly remember reading it, so I must have got it in - there is probably only two
options. I either could have got it by email, or I could have got it in hard copy. So I'm inferring
that the fact that I couldn't see an email probably means that it was given to me in hard
copy.
MR GREGGERY: Who were the six lawyers in the team - in the Social Security Branch at the
time?
MR MENZIES-McVEY: The - the three EL2s were Anna Fredericks, Gisela Aspden and Anne
Pulford. And there were - there were a couple of EL1s. Sam Willis - yes, I would need to
refresh my memory about the more junior lawyers at the time.
MR GREGGERY: Were your main dealings in this respect with Ms Fredericks and Ms Pulford?
